Anonymous Bibliometric Report Structured Abstract Purpose – This study provides a comprehensive bibliometric mapping of a corpus of 7,675 publications that sit at the intersection of machine learning and environmental science, spanning the period 2008–2022.
It aims to characterize the field’s growth trajectory, performance, social structure, conceptual landscape, and intellectual foundations.
Design/methodology/approach – A reproducible workflow was applied to a deduplicated corpus acquired from a single bibliographic source.
Performance analysis examined publication and citation trends, leading contributors, and source concentration.

Science mapping employed co-authorship, institutional collaboration, keyword co-occurrence, citation, co-citation, and bibliographic coupling networks, all constructed using association-strength normalization and Louvain community detection.
Findings – The field exhibits hyper-exponential growth, with a compound annual growth rate of 35.0% and a peak of 2,470 publications in 2022.
The Chinese Academy of Sciences is the most productive institution (366 publications), and author Fengxian Yan is a dominant hub (275 publications).
The conceptual structure is anchored by “Environmental science” and “Computer science,” with “Climate change” emerging as a central, rapidly growing theme.
Research limitations – Findings are bounded by a single-source acquisition, a 2008–2022 citation window, and metadata-only analysis.
Network visualizations are parameter-dependent and represent a filtered view of the underlying structures.

Originality/value – This report offers the first integrated, evidence-based mapping of the performance, social, conceptual, and intellectual structures of the machine learning–environmental science nexus, revealing a field that is not merely growing but undergoing a fundamental fusion of computational and environmental disciplines. --- ## 1.
This report presents a systematic, evidence-based bibliometric analysis of a corpus of 7,675 unique publications that embody this convergence.

Following established bibliometric guidelines, the study investigates four dimensions: (1) performance structure, which quantifies the productivity and impact of research constituents; (2) social structure, which maps the collaborative networks of authors and institutions; (3) conceptual structure, which reveals the thematic organization and evolution of the research; and (4) intellectual structure, which identifies the foundational works that underpin the field.

By triangulating evidence from descriptive statistics, trend analysis, and multiple network science mapping approaches, this report aims to provide a holistic portrait of a research frontier in a state of rapid and transformative growth.
Methods ### 2.1 Data Acquisition and Corpus Construction The bibliographic data were acquired from a single academic database source.
A systematic query was executed, and records were retrieved via cursor pagination until the source returned no further results, confirming complete acquisition of the 7,717 expected records.
The raw acquisition yielded 7,686 unique source records, which were subsequently subjected to deterministic exact deduplication, resulting in a final canonical corpus of 7,675 unique works.
Data Quality and Coverage The completeness of key metadata fields was assessed across the canonical corpus.
Fields critical for bibliometric analysis, including publication year, document type, source identifier, and citation counts, were present for 100% of works.
The abstract, essential for keyword extraction and conceptual analysis, was available for 74.12% of the corpus (5,689 works).
The Digital Object Identifier (DOI), a crucial persistent identifier, had a coverage of 93.84%.
These coverage rates indicate a robust metadata foundation, though the 25.88% abstract absence rate represents a limitation for full-text-dependent analyses.
Annual publication output was whole-counted by year, revealing a time span of 2008–2022.
A compound annual growth rate (CAGR) was calculated from the first to the last non-zero endpoint year.
Leading contributors—sources, authors, and institutions—were ranked by whole-counted publication frequency.

Citation impact was characterized through distributional statistics (mean, median, percentiles) and the identification of top-cited documents, with the caveat that raw counts are time-dependent and favor older publications.
Source concentration was analyzed using Bradford’s Law of Scattering, which partitions ranked sources into zones of roughly equal article productivity.

Five network types were constructed to map the field’s structures: co-authorship (social), institutional collaboration (social), keyword co-occurrence (conceptual), direct citation (intellectual), co-citation (intellectual), and bibliographic coupling (intellectual).
For each network, a candidate pool of nodes was selected based on a minimum occurrence threshold.
Edges were normalized using the association strength measure (\( c_{ij} / (w_i \cdot w_j) \)), a method well-suited for bibliometric mapping.
Communities were detected using the Louvain algorithm, with small clusters merged for interpretability.
The final visualizations represent a filtered view, displaying a maximum-spanning forest plus the strongest edges per node to highlight the backbone of each network’s structure.
A temporal overlay was applied to the keyword co-occurrence network to visualize conceptual evolution.
Growth, Productivity, and Impact The corpus is characterized by a trajectory of hyper-exponential growth.
From a modest base of 37 publications in 2008, annual output has increased nearly every year, with particularly sharp accelerations beginning in 2017.
The field peaked in 2022 with 2,470 publications, representing an 835-work increase over the previous year.
The compound annual growth rate over the entire period is 35.0%, a figure that underscores the explosive expansion of this research domain.
This growth is concentrated within a relatively small set of core sources.
The journal Remote Sensing is the dominant publication venue with 319 articles, followed by Sustainability (144) and The Science of The Total Environment (141).

The Bradford analysis confirms this concentration: a nucleus of just 40 journals (Zone 1) accounts for approximately one-third of all publications (2,474 documents), while the remaining two-thirds are scattered across 2,301 sources in Zones 2 and 3.

This pattern indicates a field with a well-defined core publishing identity, primarily rooted in remote sensing and environmental science, but with a long tail of contributions from diverse disciplinary outlets.

The Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) is the most prolific institution with 366 publications, more than double the output of the second-ranked University of Chinese Academy of Sciences (180), which is itself closely affiliated with CAS.

This dominance is mirrored in the author rankings, where Fengxian Yan tops the list with 275 publications—an output that is more than eight times greater than the second most prolific author, Shamsuddin Shahid (33 publications).

The corpus consists entirely of journal articles (100%), with no reviews or other document types identified, suggesting that the source classification may be broad or that the field’s rapid pace favors the article format for disseminating novel methods and applications.
The citation impact of the corpus is substantial but highly skewed.
The mean citation count is 44.95, while the median is considerably lower at 20.00, indicating a distribution pulled upward by a small number of highly cited works.
This is confirmed by the percentile distribution: the 90th percentile is 102 citations, and the maximum is 3,369.

Furthermore, 11.87% of the corpus (911 works) has received zero citations, a share that partly reflects the large volume of very recent publications that have not yet had time to accumulate citations.

The most-cited document, “The 30 m annual land cover dataset and its dynamics in China from 1990 to 2019” (2021), has amassed 3,369 citations, demonstrating the high impact of works that provide foundational datasets for environmental monitoring.

Other top-cited works include a seminal review on deep learning in remote sensing (3,079 citations) and a study on the global decline in evapotranspiration (2,322 citations), highlighting the dual importance of methodological guidance and empirical earth system science.
Collaboration Networks The social structure of the field is characterized by a dense, globally distributed network with a dominant Chinese hub.
The co-authorship network, filtered to 60 nodes and 120 edges, reveals a polycentric structure with 10 distinct research communities.
The most central node is Shamsuddin Shahid (weighted degree of 85), who anchors a collaborative cluster that includes Kamal Ahmed and Tarmizi Ismail, indicative of a tightly knit research group.

Fengxian Yan, despite having the highest raw publication count, appears in a separate, smaller cluster with a weighted degree of 78, suggesting a different collaborative topology—potentially a large, internally connected team where individual co-authorship links are diluted across many members.
The institutional collaboration network reinforces this picture of a Sino-centric but internationally connected field.
The network of 72 nodes and 205 edges is organized into 10 communities.

The Chinese Academy of Sciences is the undisputed central hub, with a weighted degree of 1,108, more than 75% higher than the next most central institution, the Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique (CNRS) of France (weighted degree 626).
The CAS cluster includes the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences and the Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, forming a powerful intra-national research ecosystem.
The CNRS cluster, which includes the Laboratoire des Sciences du Climat et de l'Environnement, represents a major European pole.

The network structure suggests a field where national research systems, particularly that of China, form dense internal networks that are then linked to other national and international hubs through key bridging institutions.
The keyword co-occurrence network, comprising 72 high-frequency terms and 192 edges, is partitioned into 7 distinct thematic clusters.
The two most dominant and centrally positioned keywords are “Environmental science” (4,507 occurrences, weighted degree 50,376) and “Computer science” (4,412 occurrences, weighted degree 45,247).
Their co-occurrence is the single most defining characteristic of the corpus, representing the methodological-application axis around which the entire field is organized.
Surrounding this central axis are several well-defined thematic clusters.
A prominent cluster is anchored by “Climate change” (2,555 occurrences), which is strongly linked to “Geography,” “Geology,” and “Meteorology”.
This cluster represents the application of ML to understanding and projecting climate system dynamics.
Another distinct cluster is led by “Ecology” (2,640 occurrences), which connects to biodiversity, ecosystem modeling, and conservation applications.

It shows Fengxian Yan’s work is distributed across multiple thematic veins, with the strongest links being between the author, the journal Remote Sensing, and the keywords “Environmental science,” “Geography,” and “Geology”.
This confirms that the most prolific author’s work is emblematic of the field’s core identity: applying computational methods to geo-environmental problems.
The temporal evolution of keywords reveals a field in rapid conceptual flux.

The keyword trend analysis shows that while all major themes have grown, “Computer science” has experienced the most dramatic acceleration, surpassing “Environmental science” in annual document count by 2022 (1,511 vs.
The temporal overlay on the keyword co-occurrence network provides a more nuanced view, color-coding nodes by their average publication year.

This reveals that recent research (colored toward the maximum year of ~2020.9) is concentrated in clusters related to deep learning, neural networks, and specific application domains like smart grids and building energy management.

In contrast, more established themes like “Climatology” and “Meteorology” have slightly older average publication years (~2017.6), indicating they represent a more mature, foundational layer of the conceptual structure.

Foundational Works and Knowledge Flows The intellectual structure, mapped through direct citation, co-citation, and bibliographic coupling networks, reveals a field built on a dual foundation of methodological breakthroughs and high-impact environmental datasets.
The direct citation network, with 60 nodes and 59 edges, is sparse, reflecting the fact that direct citation links among the most-cited works in a rapidly growing field are often limited.

The most central work in this network is “Using Machine Learning to Parameterize Moist Convection…” (weighted degree 45), which serves as a key node in a cluster focused on the application of ML to climate model parameterization.

The second most central is the highly cited review “Deep learning in remote sensing: A comprehensive review and list of resources” (weighted degree 38), which acts as a gateway for researchers entering the field.
The co-citation network, which connects works that are frequently cited together, provides a richer map of the intellectual base.
This network of 72 nodes and 199 edges is organized into 4 major clusters.

The most co-cited reference (weighted degree 6,771) is a work identified by its OpenAlex ID (W2911964244), which, based on its centrality and the surrounding cluster, likely represents a foundational deep learning architecture or framework that is cited across the entire field.
Other highly co-cited nodes include works on land cover classification and climate data records, forming a cluster that represents the intellectual foundation for earth observation applications.
The bibliographic coupling network, which connects documents based on shared references, reveals the current research front’s organization.
This network of 72 nodes and 193 edges is partitioned into 8 clusters.

The most central and heavily citing work is “Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning” (weighted degree 501), a high-level roadmap that integrates a vast array of methodological and applied literature.
This work anchors a cluster focused on the broad, cross-cutting application of ML to climate challenges.

Another prominent cluster is led by “Remote sensing of the terrestrial carbon cycle: A review of advances over 50 years” (weighted degree 338), which couples a body of literature on ecological remote sensing.

A third cluster, centered on “Physics-informed machine learning: case studies for weather and climate modelling” (weighted degree 276), represents a research front focused on integrating physical laws with ML models for improved climate prediction.

The 35.0% CAGR is indicative of a domain in a “hot” state, where the perceived potential of a new methodological paradigm (machine learning) to solve long-standing problems in an established discipline (environmental science) is attracting an exponentially increasing volume of research activity.
The performance and social structures reveal a field with a strong gravitational center.
The dominance of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and author Fengxian Yan is a defining feature.

This concentration of productivity, while not a measure of quality, suggests the presence of large-scale, well-resourced research programs that are capable of producing outputs at a scale unmatched by smaller groups.
The institutional collaboration network shows that this Chinese hub is not isolated; it is deeply connected to a global network, with the CNRS in France serving as a major secondary pole.
The field’s social structure is therefore best described as a globally connected network with a highly productive Sino-centric core.
The conceptual and intellectual structures reveal the nature of the fusion between the two parent disciplines.
The keyword co-occurrence network is fundamentally bipolar, with “Environmental science” and “Computer science” as the two inseparable pillars.
The temporal evolution, however, suggests a shift in the balance of this fusion.

The more rapid recent growth of “Computer science” and the concentration of recent terms in deep learning clusters indicate that the field’s cutting edge is increasingly driven by methodological innovation from the computational side.
The intellectual structure, as revealed by co-citation and bibliographic coupling, shows that this fusion is built on a canon of highly cited, primarily methodological and data-centric works.

The most-cited documents are not traditional theoretical papers but rather comprehensive reviews of deep learning methods and the release of large-scale, high-resolution environmental datasets like the 30 m annual land cover dataset of China.

The bibliographic coupling network further shows that the current research front is organized around the application of these tools to grand challenges, with “Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning” serving as a programmatic manifesto that integrates the diverse strands of the field.
The corpus was derived from a single bibliographic database, and the completeness of acquisition is relative to that source’s coverage, query, and retrieval date.
Publications not indexed in this source are absent.
The 25.88% abstract absence rate limits the comprehensiveness of keyword-based conceptual analysis.
Citation counts are a function of time.
Recent publications, particularly those from the peak year of 2022, have had minimal opportunity to accumulate citations, which skews impact metrics and the composition of top-cited lists.
All network visualizations are the result of specific, parameter-dependent choices (e.g., association strength normalization, Louvain community detection, edge reduction via maximum-spanning forest).
The classification of all 7,675 works as “articles” likely reflects the source database’s categorization scheme and may obscure the presence of review-like or other document types within the corpus.
Conclusion This bibliometric analysis reveals a research field at the intersection of machine learning and environmental science that is in a state of explosive, hyper-exponential growth.

The field’s performance structure is characterized by a highly concentrated core of prolific institutions and authors, led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Fengxian Yan, and a dominant set of journals in remote sensing and environmental science.
Its social structure is a globally connected network anchored by a powerful Sino-centric hub.

This study presents a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of climate change research published between 1990 and 2021.

Drawing on a rigorously curated corpus of 151,562 unique journal articles, we integrate performance metrics, science mapping, and network analysis to characterize the field's growth trajectory, key contributors, collaborative patterns, and conceptual evolution.
Section 2 details the reproducible methods employed.
Section 3 presents integrated findings across performance, social, conceptual, and intellectual dimensions.
Section 4 discusses the implications of these structures, and Section 5 addresses limitations.
Section 6 concludes with a synthesis of the field's current state and future directions.
Methods ### 2.1 Corpus Acquisition and Quality Assurance The bibliographic corpus was acquired through cursor-based pagination from a single source, continuing until no further results were returned.
The source reported 152,599 expected results; 152,030 unique source records were successfully acquired, representing 99.6% completeness with no truncation.
After deterministic exact deduplication, the canonical corpus comprised 151,562 unique works.
publication year, document type, cited-by count, reference count, and source identifier were present for 100% of records.
Title coverage was 99.96%, language 99.5%, and abstract 74.73%.
Digital object identifiers (DOIs) were available for 80.8% of works, and publisher information for 79.79%.
All analyses were conducted on the canonical corpus using whole counting unless otherwise specified.
Performance Analysis Annual publication output was computed by grouping works by non-missing publication year.
Compound annual growth rate (CAGR) was calculated as (final year count / initial year count)^(1 / year difference) − 1, using non-zero endpoints.
Citation metrics were derived from source-reported cited-by counts at the time of retrieval.
Bradford's law of scattering was applied by ranking sources by publication count and partitioning cumulative documents into equal thirds, with sources lacking a name excluded from zoning.

Network Construction and Analysis Five network types were constructed to map social, conceptual, and intellectual structures: coauthorship (author–author), institution collaboration (institution–institution), keyword co-occurrence (keyword–keyword), bibliographic coupling (document–document via shared references), cocitation (reference–reference via co-citation in citing documents), and direct citation (document–document via citation links).
All networks employed association-strength normalization (c_ij / (w_i × w_j)) and Louvain community detection, with small clusters merged into larger communities.

Candidate selection thresholds varied by network type: coauthorship required a minimum of 30 occurrences, institution collaboration 145, keyword co-occurrence 513, bibliographic coupling 10, cocitation 261, and direct citation 456.
Network visualizations encode node size by winsorized square-root occurrence and color by Louvain community membership.
Temporal overlays on keyword networks display mean publication year per node.
Density visualizations employ Gaussian kernel density estimation with log(1 + occurrence) weighting.
Growth, Productivity, and Impact The corpus spans 1990 to 2021, a period of extraordinary expansion in climate change scholarship.
Annual output increased from 127 publications in 1990 to 19,170 in 2021, the peak year.
This trajectory corresponds to a compound annual growth rate of 17.57%, reflecting sustained, accelerating interest.
Growth was not monotonic; the largest absolute year-over-year increases occurred in the most recent period, with gains of 3,010 publications in 2020 and 2,442 in 2021.
The corpus consists entirely of journal articles (100%), indicating that the source classification system does not distinguish reviews or other document types within this dataset.
Citation impact is highly skewed.
The mean cited-by count is 49.56, while the median is only 14.00, indicating that a small fraction of highly cited works elevates the average.
The 75th percentile is 46 citations, the 90th percentile 110, and the 95th percentile 186; the maximum observed citation count is 22,581.

Notably, 29,384 works (19.39%) have received zero source-reported citations, a proportion that partly reflects the recency of many publications, as newer works have had less time to accumulate citations.
The most-cited documents reveal the field's foundational contributions.
The highest-cited work, with 22,581 citations, is a 2008 Lancet publication on newborn survival.

Other highly cited works include "Food Security: The Challenge of Feeding 9 Billion People" (2010, 11,854 citations), "A globally coherent fingerprint of climate change impacts across natural systems" (2003, 11,212 citations), and "Ecological responses to recent climate change" (2002, 9,973 citations).
These works span food systems, biodiversity, and detection-attribution science, illustrating the multidisciplinary nature of high-impact climate research.

Keywords and Thematic Evolution The conceptual landscape of climate change research is dominated by three overarching keywords: "Climate change" (91,972 occurrences), "Geography" (90,947), and "Environmental science" (89,374).

These terms form the dense core of the keyword co-occurrence network (Figure 12), which contains 72 displayed nodes and 196 edges across 7 communities, derived from 432 candidate keywords with at least 513 occurrences.
The network reveals a well-differentiated thematic structure.

Cluster 2, the largest and most central, encompasses the core terms "Climate change," "Geography," and "Environmental science," with "Climate change" alone exhibiting a weighted degree exceeding one million.
Cluster 3 centers on "Ecology" (80,138 occurrences, weighted degree 854,889), reflecting the strong biogeophysical dimensions of climate research.
Cluster 1 is organized around "Economics" (40,653 occurrences, weighted degree 464,987), indicating a substantial social-scientific component.
Temporal analysis of keyword trends (Figure 9) demonstrates that all major thematic areas have grown in parallel with overall field expansion.

"Climate change" as a keyword appeared in 87 documents in 1990 and 10,469 in 2021; "Geography" grew from 70 to 11,142; and "Environmental science" from 84 to over 5,000 by 2005 (the last year with complete data for this keyword in the evidence bundle).

The temporal overlay on the keyword network (Figure 16) indicates that the mean publication year for displayed keywords ranges from approximately 2013.6 to 2016.9, suggesting that the conceptual core represents relatively mature terminology, with emerging terms likely falling below the occurrence threshold for network inclusion.

The keyword density visualization (Figure 17) confirms the highest density in the "Climate change"–"Geography"–"Environmental science" nexus, with secondary density peaks in ecology and economics clusters.
Foundational Works and Knowledge Bases The intellectual foundation of climate change research is revealed through cocitation, bibliographic coupling, and direct citation networks.
The cocitation network (Figure 13) contains 72 displayed nodes and 192 edges across 5 communities, from a candidate pool of 432 references with at least 261 co-citations.
The most co-cited reference (weighted degree 56,343) is an OpenAlex-indexed work (W4285719527) with 19,138 occurrences, likely representing a major IPCC report or synthesis.
Other highly co-cited works include additional OpenAlex-indexed references with weighted degrees exceeding 15,000, forming the intellectual backbone of the field.
The bibliographic coupling network (Figure 15) connects 72 documents through 197 edges across 8 communities, based on shared references among 407 candidate documents with at least 10 occurrences.

The most central documents include "Investigating soil moisture–climate interactions in a changing climate: A review" (weighted degree 545), "Dryland climate change: Recent progress and challenges" (383), and "The broad footprint of climate change from genes to biomes to people" (371).
The direct citation network (Figure 14) is sparser, with 60 nodes and 55 edges across 10 communities, from 133 candidate documents with at least 456 citations.

The most cited work within this network is "Climate Change 2007: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability," the IPCC Working Group II contribution to the Fourth Assessment Report, with 2,795 occurrences and a weighted degree of 51.
This network confirms the central role of IPCC assessment reports as organizing frameworks for the field's intellectual structure.
Journal Concentration and Dissemination Patterns Journal productivity follows a Bradford distribution, with a small core of journals contributing disproportionately to the literature.
Climatic Change ranks first with 2,093 publications, followed by The Science of the Total Environment (1,708), Sustainability (1,545), and Global Change Biology (1,359).

The Bradford analysis identifies 114 journals in Zone 1 (the core), contributing approximately 46,135 documents; 928 journals in Zone 2 (46,367 documents); and 15,883 journals in Zone 3 (46,273 documents).
This distribution indicates a mature field with a well-defined core of specialized journals, supplemented by a long tail of venues publishing climate-relevant research.

Notable among the top sources are repository-based outlets such as Zenodo (1,303 publications) and AgEcon Search (955), reflecting the inclusion of preprint and working paper repositories in the source database.
High-impact interdisciplinary journals are also prominent, including PLoS ONE (1,201), Scientific Reports (710), and Nature Climate Change (704).

Discussion The bibliometric evidence reveals a field that has undergone hyperexponential growth over three decades, with a compound annual growth rate of 17.57% that far exceeds typical scientific expansion rates.

This growth trajectory reflects both the escalating urgency of climate change as a societal challenge and the institutionalization of climate research within funding agencies, assessment bodies, and academic structures.

The gap between mean (49.56) and median (14.00) citations, combined with 19.39% uncited works, indicates that impact is concentrated among a relatively small corpus of highly influential publications.

The prominence of IPCC reports in the citation network underscores the symbiotic relationship between climate science and intergovernmental assessment processes: the IPCC both synthesizes and catalyzes research.
The social structure reveals an interesting duality.

On one hand, the coauthorship network is dominated by a single author (AGB Poore) whose extraordinary publication count (5,808) is linked to a specific repository dataset, representing a methodological artifact rather than individual research productivity in the traditional sense.

The institution collaboration network demonstrates a polycentric structure with strong European and East Asian hubs, reflecting the global distribution of climate research capacity while also highlighting the dominance of well-resourced institutions in China, France, the United States, and Australia.
The conceptual structure, as revealed by keyword co-occurrence, demonstrates that climate change research has achieved a high degree of thematic integration.

The temporal overlay suggests that this core terminology stabilized in the mid-2010s, with newer thematic directions—such as climate finance, climate anxiety, and renewable energy transitions—emerging as distinct but connected research fronts.

The intellectual structure, mapped through cocitation and bibliographic coupling, confirms that climate change research rests on a foundation of synthesis reports, detection-attribution studies, and methodological advances in modeling and impact assessment.
The bibliographic coupling network's central documents function as review and synthesis nodes, integrating knowledge across subfields and facilitating cross-disciplinary citation flows.

First, the corpus is limited to journal articles as classified by the source database; books, book chapters, conference proceedings, and grey literature are excluded, potentially underrepresenting certain disciplinary contributions.

Second, citation counts are source- and retrieval-date-dependent and do not account for differences in citation windows across publication years; recent works have had less time to accumulate citations.
Third, network centrality measures describe structural positions within the constructed networks and must not be interpreted as indicators of causal or substantive importance.
Fourth, keyword frequencies depend on source metadata practices and synonym normalization, and the abstract coverage of 74.73% limits text-mining depth.

Fifth, the extraordinary publication count of the top-ranked author reflects repository indexing practices rather than individual authorship in the conventional sense, and productivity rankings should not be equated with research quality.
Sixth, the final publication year (2021) may be incomplete, and the CAGR calculation does not establish monotonic trend.
Finally, all findings are bounded by the source database's coverage, query formulation, and retrieval date.

Conclusion This bibliometric analysis of 151,562 climate change research articles published between 1990 and 2021 reveals a field characterized by extraordinary growth, concentrated impact, polycentric collaboration, and a mature, integrated conceptual structure.
The performance structure demonstrates sustained exponential expansion, with a small core of journals and institutions contributing disproportionately to output and citation impact.
The intellectual structure rests on foundational synthesis reports and landmark studies that continue to organize citation flows across the field.

As climate change research enters its fourth decade of accelerated growth, bibliometric monitoring will remain essential for understanding the field's evolving architecture and for identifying opportunities to strengthen interdisciplinary integration and knowledge translation.

The six bibliographic coupling clusters indicate active research fronts where recent publications share common intellectual antecedents, with a strong emphasis on combined drought and heat stress effects, reflecting the field’s recognition that stresses rarely occur in isolation under field conditions.

Conclusion This bibliometric analysis reveals a rapidly growing, globally distributed research field focused on drought and heat stress in crops.

The integration of molecular genetic approaches with physiological and agronomic perspectives represents a significant maturation of the field, while the persistent fragmentation of collaboration networks suggests opportunities for enhanced knowledge integration across institutional and national boundaries.

claims.claim: Anonymous Bibliometric Report ## Abstract This report presents a bibliometric analysis of 211 unique works investigating gene-editing and stem-cell-based strategies for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
The corpus spans 2010–2023 and exhibits a compound annual growth rate of 29.90%, with output peaking at 36 publications in 2022.

The field is concentrated in a small core of journals, led by Neural Regeneration Research (13 publications), and is driven by prolific authors such as Ludo Van Den Bosch and Siddharthan Chandran (7 publications each).
the mean citation count is 46.20, while the median is 21.00, and 12.32% of works remain uncited.

Network analyses reveal a tightly integrated intellectual base organized around C9orf72 and TDP-43 pathomechanisms, with conceptual structures dominated by the intersection of genetics, disease modeling, and therapeutic development.
However, the structure, growth dynamics, and intellectual organization of this literature have not been systematically characterized.
Methods The analysis followed the bibliometric workflow outlined by Donthu et al. (2021) and employed science-mapping techniques benchmarked against bibliometrix and VOSviewer.
A deterministic, exact deduplication procedure was applied to source records, yielding a canonical corpus of 211 unique works.
the source reported 211 results, and all 211 were successfully retrieved.
Metadata completeness was assessed for ten fields; coverage exceeded 99% for DOI, language, publication date, reference count, source identifier, title, and year, while abstract coverage was 80.57%.
The temporal window was defined by the minimum and maximum non-missing publication years (2010–2023).
Annual output was whole-counted by publication year, and compound annual growth was calculated over non-zero endpoints.
Bradford’s law of scattering was applied to source productivity after excluding records without a source name.
Citation counts, which are source- and retrieval-date-dependent, were summarized using descriptive statistics.

Network analyses—coauthorship, institution collaboration, keyword co-occurrence, bibliographic coupling, and cocitation—were constructed using association-strength normalization and Louvain community detection.
Growth, Productivity, and Impact The corpus exhibits a pronounced growth trajectory.
From a single publication in 2010, annual output increased to 36 works in 2022 before declining to 30 in 2023, a year that may be incomplete at the time of retrieval.
The compound annual growth rate over the observed non-zero endpoints is 29.90%.
This expansion is not monotonic; year-over-year changes include contractions in 2017 (−5), 2020 (−6), and 2023 (−6), interspersed with surges such as the 13-publication increase in 2018.
Bradford zoning reveals that 14 journals constitute Zone 1, accounting for approximately one-third of all documents, while 69 journals populate Zone 3.
Neural Regeneration Research leads with 13 publications, followed by International Journal of Molecular Sciences (9) and Nature Communications (8).
The entire corpus consists of articles; no reviews or systematic reviews were identified in the source-supplied document types.
Citation impact is highly asymmetric.
The mean citation count is 46.20, but the median is only 21.00, indicating a right-skewed distribution.
The 90th percentile reaches 133 citations, and the maximum is 386.
Notably, 26 works (12.32%) have zero source-reported citations.
The most-cited document, “HDAC6 inhibition reverses axonal transport defects in motor neurons derived from FUS-ALS patients” (2017, Nature Communications), has accumulated 386 citations.

Other highly cited works include studies on C9orf72-mediated autophagy regulation (297 citations), RNA-targeting Cas9 for repeat expansion elimination (258 citations), and STMN2 cryptic splicing correction (256 citations).

Authors, Institutions, and Collaboration Author productivity is led by Ludo Van Den Bosch and Siddharthan Chandran, each with 7 publications, followed by Philip Van Damme (6) and Ammar Al-Chalabi, Bhuvaneish T.
Hardingham, and Wenting Guo (5 each).
The coauthorship network, constructed with a minimum occurrence of 2, contains 60 displayed nodes and 141 edges distributed across 10 Louvain communities.
The largest clusters are anchored by Chandran (Cluster 3, weighted degree 55) and Van Den Bosch (Cluster 1, weighted degree 46), reflecting two major collaborative axes.

At the institutional level, the University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School leads with 13 publications, followed by Johns Hopkins University, King’s College London, Stanford University, and the University of Edinburgh (8 each).
The institution collaboration network (71 nodes, 168 edges, 10 clusters) reveals a polycentric structure.

The University of Edinburgh and the UK Dementia Research Institute form a tightly coupled dyad (Cluster 2), while the VIB-KU Leuven Center for Brain & Disease Research anchors a distinct cluster (Cluster 1) that includes strong ties to Stanford University.
Keywords and Thematic Evolution Keyword co-occurrence analysis (minimum occurrence 5) yields a network of 72 nodes and 192 edges partitioned into 6 clusters.
The highest-weighted terms are “Biology” (occurrence 195, weighted degree 1902), “Genetics” (156, 1655), “Gene” (152, 1640), “Medicine” (141, 1452), and “Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis” (102, 1231).

These high-level terms form the backbone of the conceptual map, with “Biology” and “Genetics” co-located in Cluster 3, while “Medicine” and “Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis” reside in Cluster 2, indicating a bifurcation between fundamental genetic investigation and clinically oriented research.

Temporal keyword trends reveal that “Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis” appeared in only 1 document in 2010 but grew to 20 documents in 2022 and 16 in 2023. “Disease” followed a similar trajectory, rising from 1 document in 2010 to 18 in 2023.

The keyword overlay map (Figure 15) indicates that recent research (mean year ~2021.8) concentrates on terms associated with therapeutic development, while earlier work (mean year ~2016.2) clusters around foundational genetic and cell biology concepts.
The density visualization (Figure 16) confirms that “Biology,” “Genetics,” and “Gene” occupy the highest-density regions, representing the most saturated research areas.
Cocitation and Bibliographic Coupling The cocitation network (72 nodes, 204 edges, 5 clusters) maps the intellectual foundation of the field.

The most cocited references, identified by OpenAlex identifiers, include works on C9orf72 repeat expansions (weighted degree 853 and 829 in Cluster 4), TDP-43 pathology (weighted degree 703 in Cluster 3), and SOD1-mediated disease mechanisms (weighted degree 683 in Cluster 2).
Bibliographic coupling, which measures the shared reference profiles of the citing documents, produces a network of 72 nodes and 208 edges across 6 clusters.

The top-coupled documents include “Gene therapy for ALS: A review” (weighted degree 651, Cluster 3), “Gene Therapy in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis” (600, Cluster 2), and “Mouse models of ALS: Past, present and future” (469, Cluster 2).
The sparse construction parameters—requiring a minimum of 5 references per document and at least 2 shared references—ensure that only documents with substantive bibliographic overlap are connected.
Discussion The evidence reveals a field in rapid, though uneven, expansion.
The 29.90% compound annual growth rate and the peak in 2022 suggest sustained investment in gene-editing and stem-cell approaches for ALS.
However, the year-over-year fluctuations and the decline in 2023 may reflect funding cycles, the maturation of specific subfields, or incomplete indexing of the most recent year.
The concentration of output in a small Bradford core, led by Neural Regeneration Research, indicates that the field has a well-defined set of preferred dissemination venues.
The absence of review articles in the source-classified document types is notable and may reflect the source’s classification practices rather than a genuine absence of review content.
The citation distribution underscores the field’s translational orientation.

The highly cited works are predominantly empirical studies that established mechanistic links between genetic mutations and cellular phenotypes—such as FUS-mediated axonal transport defects, C9orf72-regulated autophagy, and TDP-43 cryptic splicing—or demonstrated therapeutic proof-of-concept, including in vivo base editing in SOD1-ALS mice and CRISPR-mediated genome editing.
The 12.32% uncited rate is consistent with a field that includes recent publications that have not yet accumulated citations.

The social structure is characterized by two dominant collaborative clusters centered on Chandran (Edinburgh) and Van Den Bosch (Leuven), with strong institutional linkages between the University of Edinburgh, the UK Dementia Research Institute, and King’s College London.

The prominence of the University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School in raw productivity (13 publications) is not fully reflected in the collaboration network’s top-weighted nodes, suggesting that its output may be distributed across multiple, less densely interconnected groups.

Conceptually, the keyword networks reveal a field organized around a core genetic vocabulary (“Biology,” “Genetics,” “Gene”) that is increasingly interfacing with disease-specific and therapeutic terminology (“Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis,” “Medicine,” “Disease”).
The intellectual structure, as revealed by cocitation and bibliographic coupling, is anchored by seminal works on C9orf72 and TDP-43 pathobiology.
The bibliographic coupling network further identifies integrative review and model-system papers that serve as connective tissue between the gene therapy, stem cell, and disease mechanism subdomains.
This structural integration suggests that the field is coalescing around a shared knowledge base, even as it diversifies methodologically.
First, the corpus is limited to 211 works retrieved from a single source at a single point in time; the completeness claim is relative to that source and query.
Second, citation counts are source- and retrieval-date-dependent and do not account for unequal citation windows; recent publications have had less time to accumulate citations.
Third, network centrality measures are descriptive of the constructed networks and parameterization and do not establish causal or substantive importance.
Fourth, keyword frequencies depend on source metadata and synonym normalization, and the final year (2023) may be incomplete.
Fifth, abstract coverage is 80.57%, meaning that 19.43% of works lack abstracts and could not contribute to content-based analyses.
Sixth, document-type labels inherit source classification practices, and the absence of reviews may be an artifact of those practices.

The field is characterized by concentrated productivity in a core of specialized journals, a highly skewed citation distribution dominated by mechanistic and therapeutic proof-of-concept studies, and a social structure organized around two major collaborative clusters.

Conceptually, the literature is transitioning from foundational genetic discovery toward therapeutic application, while intellectually, it is anchored by seminal works on C9orf72 and TDP-43 pathobiology.

claims.claim: To analyze MPs-related scientific publications from a global point of view, we created a bibliometric profile, by searching the Web of Science Core Collection database for the topic “microplastic or (micro near/1 plastic)”, in publications dated from 2004 to 2019.

The results revealed an increasing trend in publication output, and identified contributions of different countries and their collaborations, as well as influential authors and productive journals in the field of MPs research.

Using co-citation network analysis in VOSviewer, we mined cited references for knowledge bases about analytical methods, potential sources and spatial distributions of MPs, the impacts of MPs on organisms, and the interaction of MPs with contaminants, as well as microorganisms.

We also identified four global hotspots for MPs related research, using author keywords co-occurrence network analysis of all extracted publications, as well as Essential Science Indicators highly cited papers from Clarivate Analytics.

Basic Bibliometric Analysis #### 3.1.1.
Characteristics of Publication Output The year-wise distribution of publication output revealed the progress of MPs research over time (Figure 1a).
The number of publications related to MPs fluctuated slightly from 2004 to 2008, and the annual publications were all less than 100 until 2014.

Obvious growth of MPs research began in 2014, when the first United Nations Environment Assembly of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) issued the resolution UNEP/EA.1/L.8, which emphasized critical activities to address marine plastic debris and MPs challenges.
Governments worldwide began a shared commitment to addressing MPs problems and to conducting the systematic research of many aspects of MPs [30,31,32,33].
The cumulative number of annual publications since 2004 follows an exponential model (Figure 1b), and the simulation results suggest that publications about MPs issues might increase to 1703 in 2020.
On May 8, 2020, we collected data using the same TOPIC from the WoSCC database, for the time period spanning January 1, 2020 to April 30, 2020, and identified 442 relevant publications.
This value was less than the expected value for one-third of the year 2020 (567), which may be a result of the significant disruption that is being caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

Co-Authorship Network Analysis of Countries Figure 2 illustrates the collaboration network of countries conducting MPs research from 2004–2019.
The number of publications threshold was set at 30, and of the 104 countries considered, 29 met this threshold.
The whole network consisted of 29 nodes (referred to as countries) and 306 links (total link strength = 1815).
England and the USA were the most affiliated countries; their close international cooperation was indicated by 28 links and a total link strength of 353 and 369, respectively.
They were followed by Germany (links = 27, total link strength = 274), France (links = 26, total link strength = 218), and the Netherlands (links = 25, total link strength = 239).

Academic collaboration between China and the USA was far more frequent than that of any other two countries (link strength = 52), which may be attributed to the high number of Chinese postgraduates/visiting scholars studying or working on MPs research in the USA.

Anonymous Bibliometric Report Structured Abstract Purpose: This study provides a comprehensive bibliometric overview of the microplastics research domain, analyzing its performance, social, conceptual, and intellectual structures from its emergence through 2019.
A corpus of 3,973 unique journal articles was analyzed.
Performance was assessed through publication and citation metrics.
Conceptual structure was explored using keyword co-occurrence networks and temporal trends.
Intellectual structure was examined through document co-citation and bibliographic coupling networks, all employing association-strength normalization and Louvain community detection.
The field exhibits explosive growth, with a compound annual growth rate of 29.35% and a peak of 1,329 publications in 2019.
The research is concentrated in a core of environmental science journals, led by Marine Pollution Bulletin.
The social structure reveals a highly collaborative but fragmented community, with distinct Chinese and European research clusters.

Conceptually, the domain is anchored by the central theme of "Microplastics," with a clear temporal evolution from marine environmental science toward chemistry, toxicology, and human health concerns.
Within this broad concern, the study of microplastics—plastic particles smaller than 5 mm—has rapidly evolved from a niche area of marine science into a major interdisciplinary research field.
The corpus was acquired from a single bibliographic source, with cursor pagination confirming the acquisition of 3,995 unique source records from an expected 4,002 results.
After exact deduplication, the final canonical corpus comprises 3,973 unique works, all classified as journal articles.
The analysis period spans from 2004 to 2019.
Metadata completeness was assessed for key fields, revealing full coverage for critical variables like publication year, citation counts, and document type, but lower coverage for abstracts (43.32%).
Performance analysis involved descriptive statistics for annual output, source, author, and institution productivity, and citation impact.
Conceptual structure was mapped using keyword co-occurrence networks and temporal trends.
Intellectual structure was analyzed via document co-citation and bibliographic coupling networks.
All networks were constructed using association-strength normalization and Louvain community detection, with layouts optimized for clarity.
Results and Discussion ### 3.1.
Growth and Impact The microplastics research field is characterized by a period of slow, foundational growth followed by explosive expansion.
From a modest output of 28 publications in 2004, the field experienced a compound annual growth rate of 29.35% over the observed period, culminating in a peak of 1,329 publications in 2019.
This trajectory, visualized in Figure 1, shows a clear inflection point around 2015, after which annual output more than doubled every two years.
This pattern suggests the field has transitioned from an emergent phase to a period of rapid mainstream consolidation.
The citation distribution reflects this rapid growth and the presence of several highly influential, early foundational works.
The mean citation count is 201.34, but the distribution is highly skewed, with a median of 61.00.
The 90th percentile is 553 citations, and the maximum is 7,932.

A substantial portion of the corpus (22.78%, or 905 works) has received zero citations, a figure that is partly attributable to the large volume of very recent publications that have had minimal time to accumulate citations.

The most-cited documents are predominantly early reviews and empirical studies that defined the scope of the marine microplastics problem, such as "Microplastics in the marine environment" (2011, 7,932 citations) and "Microplastics as contaminants in the marine environment: A review" (2011, 5,961 citations).
Marine Pollution Bulletin is the most prolific venue with 395 publications, followed by Environmental Pollution (323) and The Science of The Total Environment (243).

A Bradford analysis reveals an extreme concentration of sources: a nucleus of just 4 journals accounts for over a third of all publications, while a long tail of 894 sources comprises the final third.
This indicates a well-defined core literature for the field.
The most prolific author is Dario Mendez-Cuadro with 127 publications, and the most productive institution is the Chinese Academy of Sciences with 109 publications.

Kardashev, suggests the corpus may contain a minor but distinct cluster of non-environmental research, possibly related to materials science, which is a limitation to be considered when interpreting thematic purity.
The co-authorship network, comprising 59 prominent nodes and 121 edges, reveals 10 distinct research communities.

The network's high modularity, with a within-between distance ratio of 0.0, indicates that while intra-cluster collaboration is strong, inter-cluster links between these major research groups are relatively sparse.
This pattern is mirrored and geographically anchored in the institutional collaboration network.
The network of 72 leading institutions forms 10 communities, with the Chinese Academy of Sciences and the Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique (CNRS) as the most central nodes.

The network structure shows a clear separation between a large European-centered cluster, which includes CNRS, Ifremer, and the University of Exeter, and a distinct Chinese cluster, comprising the Chinese Academy of Sciences, East China Normal University, and the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences.

This geographic and institutional bifurcation suggests that while the global research effort is immense, knowledge integration across these two major poles may be a challenge and an opportunity for the field's future development.

Themes and Their Evolution The conceptual core of the field is unequivocally defined by the term "Microplastics," which is the most frequent keyword with 2,770 occurrences and the most central node in the co-occurrence network.
The keyword co-occurrence network, with 72 nodes and 202 edges, is organized into 7 thematic clusters.
The largest cluster is a dense, central group of overarching environmental terms including "Environmental science," "Biology," and "Ecology," which are tightly interwoven with "Microplastics".

Surrounding this core are more specialized clusters representing distinct research sub-domains, such as a cluster focused on "Chemistry" and "Environmental chemistry," and another on "Pollution" and "Fishery".
The temporal dynamics of these keywords reveal a clear conceptual evolution.

The keyword trend analysis shows that while "Microplastics" and "Environmental science" have grown in parallel, terms like "Chemistry" and "Biology" have seen particularly sharp increases in the later years, especially from 2017 onward.
This shift is visually confirmed by the keyword temporal overlay network, where the average publication year of keywords ranges from approximately 2011.95 to 2017.89.
This indicates a maturation of the field from initial discovery and environmental monitoring toward mechanistic and impact-focused research.
Knowledge Base and Research Fronts The intellectual structure of the field, representing its knowledge base, is revealed through the document co-citation network.
This network of 72 highly cited references forms 4 distinct clusters, representing the foundational pillars of the field.

The largest and most central cluster is anchored by seminal works on the global distribution and quantification of microplastics in the marine environment, such as the reviews by Andrady (2011) and Cole et al. (2011).
These works, identified by their OpenAlex IDs, form the common intellectual ground cited across the entire domain.
The research front, representing the active areas of current investigation, is mapped by the bibliographic coupling network.
This network of 72 recent, highly referenced documents also partitions into 4 clusters, which are thematically distinct from the co-citation clusters.
The most central documents in this network are recent reviews that synthesize the state of the art and set future agendas.

The clusters in this network point to the major contemporary research frontiers: one focused on the broad environmental distribution and fate, another on freshwater and terrestrial ecosystem impacts, and a third on the ecotoxicological effects and mechanisms of harm.

The direct citation network, though sparser, confirms the central role of key empirical studies like "Accumulations of microplastic on shorelines worldwide: sources and sinks" in directly influencing subsequent work.
The corpus is derived from a single bibliographic source at a specific retrieval date, meaning citation counts are time-dependent and may not reflect the most current impact.
The final year of analysis, 2019, may be incomplete if the retrieval occurred before year-end.
Metadata coverage is imperfect; notably, only 43.32% of works include an abstract, which limits the depth of text-based analysis.

The presence of seemingly off-topic sources and authors, such as Physics of the Solid State, suggests the retrieval strategy may have introduced a small amount of noise, and findings should be interpreted with this in mind.

Network analyses are descriptive and parameter-dependent; the displayed nodes and edges are a filtered subset of the full candidate network, and centrality measures do not imply causal or substantive importance.
Finally, all productivity and citation metrics are descriptive and must not be interpreted as measures of research quality.
The performance structure shows explosive growth concentrated in a core of environmental journals, driven by a set of highly cited foundational works.
